The Government as defendant Nos.1-4 contested the suit by filling a written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land belongs to the Government as khas land and the same was settled/leased out in favour of the plaintiffs upon execution and registration of a bi-lateral deed of kabuliyat; that the suit land was also mutated in the name of the plaintiffs; that subsequently due to violation of the terms of the kabuliyat the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued a notice upon the plaintiffs on 22.03.2000 and as such the said kabuliyat was cancelled later on; that the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

 6. The predecessor of the petitioner Nos.2-6 as added defendant No.7 also contested the suit by filling another written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Satish Chandra Das, who granted settlement of the same along with other lands in favour of Azhar Ali Miah and Mozahar Ali Miah; that in order to recover arrear rents for 1360-1362 BS from the said tenants Azhar and Mozahar, Satish Chandra filed Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 in the Court of the then Munsif, Goalando and that suit was compromised between the parties on 26.02.1957; that pursuant to the said compromise decree, Azhar and Mozahar were admitted as tenants and they remained in possession of the suit land as owner thereof; that Azhar Miah died leaving behind widow Khodeja, 2 sons-Abdul Latif and Golam Sarwar and one daughter Jahanara Begum as his heirs; that the said heirs of Azhar Ali transferred the suit land in favour of the added defendant No.7 by a registered sale deed being No.4239 dated 15.06.1982 and delivered possession in his favour; that the suit land became uncultivable because of situation by the flood of 1988; that the ancestral/paternal residence of the plaintiff's was in Sujanagar, Pabna  and because of destruction of their house in Pabna by a flood in 1988, they stared looking for a piece of land for residential purposes; that the plaintiffs are the distant relatives of the said defendant No.7 and therefore, the latter allowed the former to live in the suit land on a temporary basis given the uncultivable nature of the suit land and accordingly, the plaintiffs erected homestead in the suit land in the first part of 1989 and started living therein and planted various trees; that at that time the plaintiffs undertook to vacate the suit land soon after they get another piece of suitable land; that in the middle of November, 2000 they claimed title to the suit land on the basis of a kabuliyat from the Government and that even being requested to vacate the suit land the plaintiffs refused to do so and as such the said defendant filed Title Suit No.214 of 2000 against the plaintiffs in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sader, Rajbari praying for a decree for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession; that the suit land is not at all the khas land of the Government and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 11. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, learned advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners took me to the revisional-4 application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, the disposition of all the P.W.s and D.W.s and the documents exhibited by the parties and submits that the plaintiffs as well as the Government miserably failed to prove that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S.A. operation in view of the fact that neither the plaintiffs nor the Government adducted any minimum iota of evidence including the khas khatian itself before the courts below in support of their contention nor did they disclose the source through which or the basis on which or the manner in which the suit land devolved upon the Government and as such the plea of khas khatian which is the genesis of the plaintiffs' claim falls flat and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan drew my attention to Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and referred to the decision of Geeta Rani alias Shamima Khatun vs. Bangladesh, 36 DLR (AD) 225; Bangladesh and others vs. Mallick Ali Ahmed and others 3 CLR (AD) 345 and Md. Kalam Mollah and others vs. Sheikh Samsu and others, 23 BLT 320, which will be discussed later on. 

 12. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan also submits that although the Government (defendant Nos.1-4) filed written statement and cross-examined the defendants' witnesses (DWs), they did not adduce any evidence of their own in support of their contention and as such their contention as raised in their written statement having not been supported/proved by any other evidence, oral or documentary, their written statement is liable to be discarded/kept out of consideration. In this regard Mr. Bhuiyan refers to the decisions of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs. Hosne Ara Begum and others, 34 BLD 55; Asgar Ali Mia and others vs. Bangladesh and others, 16 BLC 37 and Sreejukta Haladhar Karmakar and others vs. Bangladesh and others, 16 BLD 519. 

 20. On the other hand, Mr. Shah Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 submits that on and from 14` April, 1956 the rent receiving interest of all the rent receivers in Bangladesh having been acquired by the Government under Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the SAT Act), the defendant-petitioners' claim of title to the suit land on the strength of a compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 drawn up in Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 between the then Zamindar/landlord Satish Chandra Das and his tenants Mohammad Mozahar Ali Miah and Azhar Ali Miah from whom the petitioners got the suit land by way of successive transfers becomes barred by law. In support of his submission, Mr. Hossain referred to the decisions reported in 31 DLR (AD) 323; 14 BLC 848; 38 DLR (AD) 93 and 20 DLR 699. Amongst the cited decisions, I feel the necessity to quote the ratio decidendi of the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensing vs. Abani Kanta Chakraborty and others 38 DLR (AD) 93, which runs as follows : 

 "After the abolition of all rent receiving interests in the country there is only one class of tenancy under the Government whose rights and liabilities are governed by an uniform law." 

 21. Controverting the above submission readily, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 was filed by the then Zaminder Satish Chandra Das for realizing the arrear rent in respect of the suit land for 1360-1362 BS (corresponding to 1953-1955) and the said Rent Suit having been field within 3 (three) years for realizing the arrear rents for the period before Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force, the said Rent Suit is maintainable within the meaning of Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 and therefore, the compromise decree drawn up in that suit is legal, whereby the landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azhar Ali as his tenants for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioners having acquired title to the suit land by successive transfers by dint of 3(three) separate registered sale deeds of 1961, 1982 and 2000 from them and their transferees, are the lawful title holders of the suit land. 

 26. It is the case of the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 and the Government (defendant Nos.1-4) that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S.A. operation, but neither the plaintiffs nor the Government adduced any evidence including the khas khatian itself before the Courts below in support of their contention. Again, although the Government filed a written statement, they did not adduce any evidence, oral or documentary, to show as to when, why and how the suit land became khas in their name and as such the written statement of the Government will not ipso facto be admissible in evidence unless and until the same is supported by competent witness of convincing nature, and as such Section 92 of the SAT Act as well as the decisions referred to by the defendant: petitioners will stand in the way of the claim of plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 as well as the Government. At this juncture I think it is necessary to quote Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, which runs as follow: 

 (a) when he dies intestate leaving no heir entitled to inherit under the law of inheritance to which he is subject; 

 It is pertinent to mention here that the Government did not turn up before the Courts below as well as this Court in the course of the Rule hearing to establish its claim to the suit land and therefore, the plaintiffs as well as the Government signally failed to prove that the suit land ever vested in the Government as khas land in view of the Government's failure to adduce evidence in support of its written statement. This view finds support from the case of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs, Hosne Ara Begum and others 34 BLD 55, wherein it has been held that: 

 "The filing of the written statement without giving any oral testimony in support of the same before the Court below and without facing cross-examination the same will not be considered ipso facto as evidence, rather, either of the pleadings must be proved by giving oral evidence." 

 It also appears from the abovementioned compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 that landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali as his tenants for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioners having acquired their title to the suit land by successive transfers by dint of 3(three) separate registered sale deeds dated 01.03.1961 (Ext.2 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000), 15.06.1982 (Ext.5 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000) and 16.07.2000 (Ext.3 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000) from them and their transferees, are the lawful title holders of the suit land. 

 Furthermore, the plaintiffs stated in paragraph 7 of the plaint that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari (defendant No.4 to the suit) by his letter dated 12.03.2000 merely threatened to cancel their kabuliyat, but at no point of time their lease was actually cancelled, and the threat of cancellation as opposed to any actual cancellation is merely an apprehension which cannot substitute the cause of action of the suit as framed and therefore, the suit is premature and liable to be dismissed as being not maintainable in law as per the decision given in the case of Kamaluddin (Md.) and another vs. Secretary, Ministry of Land, Bangladesh and others 56 DLR (AD) 212, wherein it has been held that: 

 33. On perusal of the pleadings, evidence and other materials on record, I am of the considered view that the judgment of the trial Court is very much sound, proper and in accordance with law for the reasons stated above and it does not suffer from any Misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration or misconstruction of any document affecting the merit of the case and as such I find no reason to interfere with the same. On the other hand, the Court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the provisions of law, the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision by failing to apply its judicial mind to the given set of facts and as such it failed to independently assesses the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure since it turned down the decision of the trial Court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial Court and thus, the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside.
